doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Finding a niche in traditional jazz: Condon's, Giordano, Wilber, Goodman
summary: Contrasting himself with Brecker's listening, he built a tune list, subbed for Ed Polcer at Condon's and got work with Giordano, Wilber, Goodman and the jazz party circuit.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So after the trumpet became part of you again, you entered into the competitive scene in New York City?
When I look at the Local 802 book I see page after page of trumpets, page after page of saxophones.

Well they’re mostly part-time guys. Well see the thing was that I was able to find a niche. I mean this is kind of interesting because this is sort of where this thing developed in my career, which has been kind of a blessing and a curse. Because now my orientation, when I left college — I went to college with Michael Brecker and I mean the stuff he was listening to then, his listening habits were a little more advanced than mine, I would say when we were in school, when we were like 18 or 19. I’d say mine were a little broader than his. But he was like really honing in on Coltrane, the latest stuff, stuff that Wayne

Shorter or Miles was doing. Just when these records came out he had them. He was like listening to them day and night. And so that was part of it. When I was in college I mean Freddie Hubbard was my idol. I loved Freddie Hubbard and I liked to play in that sort of way. Well when I’m in New York and now it’s like early 80s, I just decided that I wanted to play and I wanted to take any jobs I could and get as close to jazz work as possible. Well at that time I just found this niche working in traditional jazz, which I didn’t know existed. I didn’t know that I was going to become a part of it. But the thing is because I had started out listening to that music and it was so much a part of my consciousness — you know, Louis, Bix, those tunes. I remember sitting down and making a tune list, because Ed Polcer was working at Eddie Condon’s. This was the last Eddie Condon’s on 54th Street. And he was always looking for subs and there just weren’t that many guys, especially younger guys, who knew the stuff. And so I just wrote down a list of tunes, of the old tunes. And I was — it just kind of astounded me how many of them I just knew already. So that was an advantage right there. So then I’m working at Condon’s and then I’m kind of in this freelance pool and working with Vince Giordano’s Night Hawks and then Bob Wilber and then Benny Goodman and all of that. And at that time I mean maybe because there was a sort of stigma, there always has been except maybe until very recently, about playing — I mean there still is to an extent — playing older styles. There were just very few people doing it. Also the original, the guys of that generation who were doing it, they were getting in their 60s, 70s, 80s. If they weren’t dead they were like out of commission. And I would get work that way. For instance I can remember a tour that Billy Butterfield was supposed to do and he had some health problems and so I had to step in and do it. Things like that. And that sort of got me into the jazz party circuit and here I am now. And now, like I should make it clear, I’ve always had this emotional connection to this music, to that style, or those styles. I mean it’s a pretty broad spectrum in itself. But there’s always been this other part of me too that has wanted to do really creative things and not imitate Freddie Hubbard or Woody Shaw but like do stuff that nobody else is doing.
